findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity denial cache collisions
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey (pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:30-32) builds the denial cache key from namespace, userUID, action, name and parent, but not from the identity type. In Service.Check (service.go:116) the key is computed from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw UID portion of the subject. Two different identity types can share the same UID string (e.g. subject 'user:abc' and 'service-account:abc' both yield UserUID 'abc'; anonymous and render subjects are also validated to produce a UID). A denial cached for one identity type is then returned as a denial for a different identity type with the same UID, incorrectly denying access. The key must include checkReq.IdentityType (and the same fix applies wherever the denial key is constructed).

findings.title: Denial cache is populated from stale cached permissions, permanently denying access after a permission grant

However, the more serious issue is the ordering combined with the denial cache check at line 116-121: once a denial entry exists for (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent), every subsequent Check for that exact tuple returns Allowed:false for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) without ever consulting the permission cache or the DB. If a permission is granted (e.g. the creator is assigned a role on the dashboard they just created, which is the exact scenario this PR targets), the user is still denied until the denial entry expires, and — because the denial cache is checked before the permission cache — the newly granted permission is never observed during that window. Additionally, when the cached permission map exists but the specific resource is not in it (line 124-136), the code re-queries the DB, but if the DB query also returns not-allowed, the denial is cached even though the earlier cached-permission miss may have been caused by a stale negative; combined with the fact that permCache entries are only refreshed on the getUserPermissions path, a denial recorded against a stale permission snapshot can outlive the snapshot. The denial cache should be invalidated (or not written) when permissions change, and the TTL should be treated as a security-relevant bound; at minimum the denial entry must be keyed consistently with the permission cache generation so a permission update clears it.

As written, a transient store error in GetUserIdentifiers is hidden and the request proceeds to getIdentityPermissions, which will fail again with a less specific error path and inflate error metrics.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented twice on the cached-permission path, double-counting cache hits
findings.body: In Service.Check, when getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeds and checkPermission returns allowed, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage is incremented at line 132; but line 137 unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage with 'false' (cache miss) after the if-block whenever the cached path did not return early — including the case where the cached permissions existed but the specific resource was not in them and the code correctly falls through to the DB. More importantly, the metric semantics are now wrong: line 137 reports a cache miss even when the permission map was found in cache (the miss was only for the specific resource scope, not the permission cache). The 'false' increment should only happen when getCachedIdentityPermissions actually returned cache.ErrNotFound, and the resource-level miss should either not count as a permission-cache miss or be tracked with a distinct label. As written, dashboards/metrics for cache hit ratio are corrupted.

findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck (service_test.go:893-996) covers allow-from-cache, DB fallback on miss, DB fallback on outdated cache, and deny-on-explicit-denial-entry, but it never tests the dangerous interactions introduced by this PR: (1) that a denial entry for one resource does not deny a different resource (the key-collision issue from the unescaped '_' concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey); (2) that a denial entry recorded for one identity type/subject form does not deny a different identity type with the same UID; (3) that after a denial is cached, a subsequent grant (permission added to the store) is honored once the denial expires or is otherwise invalidated — i.e. the test suite gives no confidence that the denial cache cannot lock a user out after a legitimate grant. findings.body: In the 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest (service_test.go:982), the permission cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. The production code only ever stores 'true' values in the scope map (getScopeMap, service.go:569-579, sets permMap[perm.Scope] = true), so a 'false' entry is not a state the code can produce.
